title: Merry Christmas in Polish: Wesołych Świąt and Card Wishes
excerpt: Merry Christmas in Polish is Wesołych Świąt. Learn to pronounce it, reply with Nawzajem, write card wishes and say Happy New Year.
metaDescription: Merry Christmas in Polish is Wesołych Świąt. Learn to pronounce it, reply with Nawzajem, write card wishes and say Happy New Year.
summary: Wesołych Świąt (veh-SOH-wihkh shfyohnt) is the everyday way to say merry Christmas in Polish; Wesołych Świąt Bożego Narodzenia is the full, formal version.
The greeting is plural and in the genitive because Poles celebrate several days of Święta and the hidden verb życzę (I wish) takes the genitive.
Reply with Nawzajem! or Wzajemnie!, and say happy New Year with Szczęśliwego Nowego Roku or the old-fashioned Do siego roku.
Ready-to-copy card wishes cover friends, family and formal contacts, plus Easter greetings like Wesołego Alleluja.

authorBio: PolishPal Contributor writes about Polish culture, history, and language for learners and the Polish diaspora.
factNotes: Do siego roku: sources confirm 'siego' is the genitive of the archaic pronoun si/sia/sio meaning 'this' (NCK), and Wiktionary glosses the phrase as 'do tego roku (obyśmy dożyli)' / 'till the next year'. No source gave a fuller historical reconstruction, so the article presents only that and says it is 'usually explained' as a wish to live to see the coming year. Swapped 'bogatego Mikołaja' for 'hojnego Mikołaja' because only the latter was found in a source. Wigilia (24 Dec) as a statutory day off since 2025 is from infor.pl/pit.pl reports of the amended holidays act; I did not open the Dziennik Ustaw text itself. The capitalisation of 'Świąt' in greetings is described as common practice, not as a dictionary rule. Fireworks photo is a generic city (not Poland) and is captioned without claiming a location; the Easter-egg photo is not claimed to be Polish.
